entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's ... it's says it's supposed to be used ... the original deed said that the property was to be used for educational purposes, the one in 1900.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have any restrictions that it would revert back to the landowner?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't believe so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did Camp Adair, did they own that property during World War II?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that property was given to the school and then after it stopped being a school it went directly into the Farmer's Union and the Farmer's Union transferred it directly to the Foundation?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's only had three owners?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Since the Moores?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's ... and as far as you know there's no restriction on the use of the property and the Foundation can do whatever they want with it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's restricted to historical educational uses. It is, because the Farmer's Union let us have the deed if we would continue using it the way we were using it when we leased it, and we were having historical exhibits with old desks and slates and we'd show spinning or historical craft or wild flower or what ... one time we had the Heart of Valley show the development of the Willamette Valley. And so we got the deed with the condition that we continue to use it as a historical educational purpose.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that allow you to sell and take the money and buy a bunch of history books and give them to the college? All I'm curious about are the restrictions as people have transferred this

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: property and there's a neighboring landowner that might be able to change the use or the Foundation members that come after your time that might alter the intent or the purpose of the Foundation, is that possible?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not if we get it on the National Historic Register, I don't think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't think so either, but I'm just curious.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that National Historic ... we're still working on it, but Louise's husband, she's doing the typing of the significance narrative and her husband had a stroke and so she was just starting to type it and so she said she needed a month or so to get ... and so after Christmas. This last deed that we got from the Farmer's Union said that if we let's see ... if we didn't keep the property it would go to the Benton County 4-H Association or a similar youth activity or other non-profit organization. So that we were talking about that at the last board meeting, and said it would be like the Benton County Historical Society because that's the closest that we ... to us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So if your Foundation disintegrated you would probably be your last act of the Foundation to donate it to the Historical Society?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In our constitution bylaws, "upon the winding up and dissolution of the this corporation after paying or adequately providing for the debts and obligations of their organization, the remaining assets shall be distributed to a non-profit fund, foundation or corporation." So that would be like the Benton County Historical Society.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you could amend it or if you decided to keep your

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And one of the first amendment, "this corporation is organized exclusively for historical educational purposes, or within the meaning of this."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Such things as this tour, would count

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say so, it is historical education.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've gone through all my questions and covered all the way from 1900 on the school and before 1900 on your family and we up to the present and gone into the future what could happen. Do you see anything in your notes that to talk about at this time? After it's transferred, you'll have another opportunity to go through this and add and amend.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can't think of anything, we're still planning to go ahead with maybe the fun run again this year. We need to raise about $4500 more for the putting our foundation under the building, so we're still moving forward.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your main purpose or short term objective, I should say, is right now is to get a foundation under the building and for that will need to raise four or five thousand dollars. So that's kind of the focal point at this time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We need, actually we need about $8500 and we have almost $5000, and that's from donations and fund raisers the last couple of years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Come full circle, the Foundation got organized to put a roof on the building and put electricity in and now you're trying to put a basement under the roof and take the electricity out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right. Yeah, it's a fun project to work on, I think it brings the community together, you know, that you won't know all these people if you weren't working on the Foundation. And a lot of people ... if people are stopping there, they'll check in and see if they're going to damage it or something and so ... I don't know what's going to happen when a whole lot of people start using it and I don't know what we'll do because so far it's just a few people using it, like once in a while an art group will come out and make a painting of it or something. One time

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You don't want it loved to death, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right. I think there's such a thing as ... tromping ... too much tromping ... the floor ... the two school houses I visited back in Iowa when we were there three or four years ago that were set up as historic sites did not let you go

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: into the school house, you looked in from the outside and because if you take hundreds of people walking through all the time, bit by bit it will just ... the floor will just be ground to bits. And I thought so far ... I mentioned this at several board meeting ... so far we're letting people walk through it, we were wondering if we would need to restrict the number of people in there at a time particularly like if you have this large group that comes out maybe just ten to twelve in there at a time and then have them go through and then another group, because we may someday have to be at the point where we can just let people look in the door, you know, not walk through it. Maybe it will be so disintegrated these Oregon rains, you know. Things don't last forever.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I know ... covered bridges and that's the problem we have here is the weather. It's a problem everywhere. Cultural resource management ... everything has an end at some point. Seems like a lot of what we're doing is to delay that end as much as possible. I know that you've made detailed drawings of the rafter and the different structural elements and you're trying to recreate the paint, has there been any discussion perhaps of having school group such as the Oregon State College that study management to make recommendations or to work with the Foundation in developing management funds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we haven't tried that, everybody's kind of do-it- yourselfers so they always say "we can do it, we don't need them. We can do it." So, a lot of people are inexperienced

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: but they're willing to volunteer and so we haven't really tried any long philosophical plans with what are we going to do ten or twenty years from now. We just say, well, "can you paint next Saturday" you know, or "can you come down and help clean" and we called a bunch of people we know to help come and clean. It's kind of a basic do-it-yourself er thing. You do ... things don't move as fast, I think, when you have volunteers like we have to wait for Louise's husband to get better so she can type this. Louise Hollister, she's got to have a cataract operation so we have to wait a few weeks until she can help, you know. So you kind of move a little slower, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe that's one of the better things after volunteers, is that people are putting out what they can and there's not the pressure.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and they care about it. Things aren't as structured, you know, as in the bigger more organized museums probably. Maybe we should be getting more professional. Bill Lewis says the more professional you get, you know, the better we don't have a training, like up at Aurora they train their hostesses that show people through, training social ... we just have a neighbor who comes down there, you know, you just kind of pour the punch or something and we're not polished professional people, we just kind of ... neighbors just kind of doing it because nobody else has done it. We think it's a beautiful spot and we want to save it and so we just do it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I guess that's the last question I can think of ... When you moved in, it was mostly people from Oregon State, most of them and then Hewelett-Packard came in and there was an influx of people, professionals from Hewelett-Packard. Have you notice any other trends of population, would that still pretty much characterize the background of the present population, high educated, well educated people from campus or Hewelett-Packard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there aren't a lot of campus ... well, there are a few campus people but there are a lot of like high school teachers and I'm not so sure Deardorffs are with the Bureau of Mines in Albany and

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Fish and Wildlife?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Fish and Wildlife, and Woodcock is a sales ... works in office for an oil company, his wife is an insurance person.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Lot of government, a lot of educators, a lot of well educated people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say most of them are pretty well educated. I would say we've seen fewer like old rancher types.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any operating ranches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this valley we from an agricultural background to then a military base and a large share of it is now a lot of rural, well

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: educated professional ... so the demographics ... that was a real change.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Big change. Maybe John ... Bruce Johnson down here owns a lot of property and has cattle, but he also works at Hewelett-packard. So it's still a sideline.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: His main income, his main professional focus is Hewelett-Packard rather than cattle ranching?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right, but

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's interesting.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He does probably have the biggest spread of anybody in the Valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many head does he have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, but his property is Dolan's and Hollister's and now he's renting Daily's and his

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Does he have dozens or hundreds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he doesn't have hundreds. Probably between fifty and hundred.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Have you noticed any trends or changes in wildlife population, I know I gave you an article on a cougar that have spotted here, are there black bear in the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was once just shortly before we came here. Louise Hollister said her husband shot a bear out here ... I don't

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: know why he shot it, but there was one out here in their yard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Opossum or raccoon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We have lots of those.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: More or less or just about the same? Do you think it's a fairly stable population, wildlife population?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know since they come out at night, but everybody has them. We've seen porcupine, we see a lot of deer, and squirrels.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: More deer now than before or about the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I couldn't compare, I think there's still a lot of deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about beaver, are they still ... have they been trapped out of the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I haven't been on that section of creek up there, I should have asked Ted because he went last Sunday, but I think they built a dam along the main road and then people got worried, that moved in down there, that it was going to flood the road Sulphur springs Road, so they may have been moved.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How big were the fish the kids caught?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, six inches.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ever get any over a foot?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Little.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That covers just about everything I can think of, how about you? I sure appreciate it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Thank you.

entries.text: APPENDIX: PERSONAL BIOGRAPHY

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was born on a farm in Iowa, attended country school for nine years, graduated from Iowa City High Scool, and then attended Iowa State College, studying textiles and clothing. In my early years I helped with farm work, milking cows, gathering eggs, driving horses on the hay wagon, hand shelling ear corn, etc. We made clover leaf chains, dug for crawdads at our creek, climbed in the hayloft, and hung May baskets for fun. I attended Sunday School and 4-H Club during my childhood.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I taught in a one room rural school for two years and a small town school one year.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At college I met Don Grabe. We married and had three children.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We moved out West in 1968 to Oregon. We now live on a wooded acreage in the beautiful Soap Creek Valley with our collie dog and two horses. Many birds and flowers add distinctive charm to this hillside homesite.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have studied art for many years at LBCC (Linn-Benton Community College) and have done watercolors and calligraphy. I have also studied Spanish, Portuguese, and piano.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Living a short distance from the old Soap Creek School #32, I became interested in historical restoration, and have helped collect old photos, histories, early school text books, slates, and desks since 1974. Saving this precious heirloom (the school, its grounds, and contents) for future generations is an important goal in my life.

entries.speaker: A
